text: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh. I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, so that I may perform these signs of mine among them,
and so that you may tell your children and grandchildren how harshly I dealt with Egypt and what signs I did among them, and you will know that I am the LORD."

So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said to him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, so that they may serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go, then tomorrow I will bring locusts into your land.
They will cover the face of the ground so that no one can see the land. They will devour what little you have left after the hail, and they will strip every tree that grows in your fields.

They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and of all the Egyptians—something neither your fathers nor your forefathers have ever seen from the day they first came to be on the earth until now." Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.

versions.text: They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and of all the Egyptians—something neither your fathers nor your forefathers have ever seen from the day they came into this land until now." Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says "from the day they were upon the ground/land," i.e., from the beginning of their existence on the land, not from the day they entered or arrived in it. "Came into this land" adds an idea of immigration that is not in the text.

versions.text: They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and of all the Egyptians—something neither your fathers nor your forefathers have ever seen from the day they first lived on this land until now." Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew הָאֲדָמָה here has no demonstrative and in this idiom refers to the earth/ground in general (the span of human existence), not specifically to the land of Egypt. "On this land" narrows the sense and introduces a demonstrative not present in the source. The revision keeps the earlier correction (existence rather than immigration) while removing the added "this."

text: Pharaoh's officials said to him, "How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may serve the LORD their God. Don't you see yet that Egypt is ruined?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. "Go, serve the LORD your God," he said. "But just who is going?"
Moses answered, "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a festival to the LORD."
Pharaoh said, "The LORD be with you—if I ever let you go along with your children! Clearly you are bent on evil.
No! Let the men go and serve the LORD, since that is what you have been asking for." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.

Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt to bring the locusts. Let them come up over the land of Egypt and devour every plant in the land, everything the hail has left."
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD sent an east wind across the land all that day and all that night. By morning the wind had brought the locusts.
They swarmed over all the land of Egypt and settled in every part of the country in vast numbers. Never before had there been such a swarm of locusts, nor will there ever be again.

They covered the face of the whole land until it was black. They devoured every plant in the land and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green remained on tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.
Now forgive my sin just this once, and pray to the LORD your God to take this deadly plague away from me."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.

And the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind, which carried the locusts away and swept them into the Red Sea.[^1]

[^1]: Hebrew: the Sea of Reeds.

versions.text: And the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind, which carried the locusts away and swept them into the Red Sea. Not one locust was left anywhere in Egypt.
versions.explanation: A brief footnote noting that the Hebrew reads "Sea of Reeds" would help readers, since the traditional rendering "Red Sea" is an interpretation of the Hebrew name.

text: But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let the Israelites go.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and darkness will come over the land of Egypt—a darkness that can be felt."
So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one left his place for three days. Yet all the Israelites had light where they lived.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD. Only your flocks and herds must stay behind; even your children may go with you."

versions.text: Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD. Even your children may go with you; only leave your flocks and herds behind."
versions.explanation: The clauses have been reversed. The Hebrew puts the restriction first and the concession second, which builds the rhetorical force of Pharaoh's offer; restoring the order also reads naturally aloud.

text: But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings to present to the LORD our God.
Our livestock must go with us too; not a hoof is to be left behind. We have to use some of them in serving the LORD our God, and until we get there we will not know what we are to offer to the LORD."
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he was unwilling to let them go.
Pharaoh said to Moses, "Get away from me! Make sure you never appear before me again, for on the day you see my face you will die."
"Just as you say," Moses replied. "I will never appear before you again."
